nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

flashcards.front: What does DNS do?
flashcards.back: Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

questions.q: Two Azure VNets are in the SAME REGION. Workloads in VNet-A need LOW-LATENCY (≤ 1 ms), high-bandwidth PRIVATE connectivity to a shared database in VNet-B. The link must use the Microsoft backbone, NOT IPsec encapsulation. Operating overhead must be minimal. Which connectivity option fits all three constraints?
choices: VNet peering between the two VNets in the same region
A site-to-site VPN gateway pair, one in each VNet, tunnelling traffic between them
An ExpressRoute private peering circuit terminated into both VNet gateways
An Azure Virtual WAN hub with both VNets connected as spokes
questions.explanation: Same-region VNet peering routes traffic directly over the Microsoft backbone with sub-millisecond latency and no gateway hop in the data path — exactly the low-latency, low-overhead private link the scenario requires. A site-to-site VPN gateway pair adds IPsec encryption overhead and a VPN gateway hop on each side, raising latency. ExpressRoute is designed for on-prem-to-Azure private connectivity, not VNet-to-VNet inside the same region. Virtual WAN routes through a managed hub, which adds at least one extra hop and is intended for global multi-region transit.

questions.q: A VM has both a SUBNET NSG and a NIC NSG attached. An INBOUND packet to port 443 arrives at the VM. In what order are the two NSGs evaluated for the inbound direction?
choices: NIC NSG first, then Subnet NSG
Subnet NSG first, then NIC NSG
Whichever NSG has more specific rules is evaluated first
Both NSGs are evaluated in parallel and the more permissive rule wins
questions.explanation: For inbound traffic to a VM, the Subnet NSG is evaluated first, then the NIC NSG; the order reverses for outbound. Both NSGs must allow the packet — a deny in either one drops it. 'NIC first then subnet' is the outbound order, not inbound. Specificity does not change evaluation order — both NSGs always run, in a deterministic direction-dependent order. NSGs are not evaluated in parallel, and the engine uses 'either deny blocks' semantics, not 'most permissive wins'.

questions.q: A team needs browser-based, SSH/RDP access to Azure VMs WITHOUT (a) opening port 22/3389 to the internet, (b) deploying or operating any additional VMs (jump-boxes), and (c) installing client software. Which Azure service meets all three?
choices: Deploy a jump-box VM with a public IP and open RDP/SSH on it
Enable Just-in-Time VM access through Microsoft Defender for Cloud
Provision Azure Bastion as a managed PaaS jump host
Add an NSG rule allowing RDP only from the corporate IP range
questions.explanation: Azure Bastion is a managed PaaS jump host: users open the VM in the Azure portal, Bastion proxies RDP/SSH over TLS from the browser, ports 22/3389 stay closed to the internet, and no client software or jump-box VM is needed. A self-managed jump-box VM violates the 'no extra VM' constraint and still exposes RDP/SSH publicly. Just-in-Time VM access opens management ports for a short window from the user's IP — it still requires public listeners and a local RDP/SSH client. An NSG rule limiting source IPs narrows exposure but leaves RDP/SSH open and still requires a client.

questions.q: An application subnet must force ALL outbound internet-bound traffic through a third-party firewall NVA at 10.0.1.4 before it leaves Azure. The NVA must intercept, inspect, and then forward. Which configuration achieves this?
choices: An outbound NSG rule denying 0.0.0.0/0 on the application subnet
Enable IP forwarding on the application VMs' network interfaces
A User-Defined Route 0.0.0.0/0 → Virtual Appliance 10.0.1.4 on the subnet
VNet peering with gateway transit between the application and NVA VNets
questions.explanation: A User-Defined Route with next-hop 'Virtual Appliance' and the NVA's private IP overrides Azure's default system routes and steers traffic to the firewall. The route table is attached to the application subnet, and IP forwarding must be enabled on the NVA's NIC (not the application VMs'). An NSG rule filters traffic but cannot redirect it. Enabling IP forwarding on the app VMs lets them forward traffic for other hosts but does not change their outbound next hop. Peering with gateway transit provides connectivity between VNets but does not change the default route to the internet.

questions.q: A team is choosing between Basic and Standard Load Balancer SKUs for a zone-redundant, multi-AZ deployment. They need: (a) frontends and backend pools that survive an AZ outage, (b) HA Ports for active/standby NVAs. Which statement about the SKUs is correct?
choices: Standard SKU supports internal-only frontends with zone redundancy; Basic supports both internal and external
Standard SKU requires a VPN gateway for zone-redundant failover; Basic does not
Standard SKU supports zone-redundant frontends and backends across availability zones; Basic is not zone-aware
Standard SKU is capped at 100 backends; Basic supports unlimited zone-redundant backends
questions.explanation: Standard Load Balancer is the zone-aware production SKU: zone-redundant and zonal frontends, multi-AZ backend pools, HA Ports, secure-by-default, and pools up to 1000 instances. Basic Load Balancer is not zone-aware — its frontends and backend pool live in a single zone — and is being retired in 2025. The 'internal only' framing inverts the actual support matrix. Neither SKU requires a VPN gateway for redundancy. Standard scales much higher than Basic, not the other way around.

questions.q: VMs in a VNet must resolve internal hostnames like `appserver.internal.contoso.com` to private IPs WITHOUT operating any DNS server VM. The zone must be authoritative for `internal.contoso.com` and visible only inside linked VNets, with VMs auto-registering their A records. Which feature?
choices: An Azure Private DNS zone linked to the VNet with auto-registration enabled
Azure-provided DNS using the default *.internal.cloudapp.net suffix
A public Azure DNS zone linked to the subscription
A Windows Server DNS VM with the VNet's custom DNS pointed at it
questions.explanation: An Azure Private DNS zone is authoritative for a custom domain, scoped to linked VNets, and with auto-registration enabled Azure adds A records for each VM automatically — no DNS VM, no manual record management. Azure-provided DNS uses the fixed *.internal.cloudapp.net suffix and is not authoritative for a custom zone. A public Azure DNS zone answers on the internet rather than being scoped to a VNet and offers no auto-registration. A Windows Server DNS VM works in principle but violates the 'no DNS server VM' constraint and requires custom scripting to mimic auto-registration.

questions.q: A global SaaS app has backends in East US AND West Europe. Requirements: route users to the geographically closest HEALTHY backend; fail over instantly to the other region on backend failure; terminate TLS at the edge with WAF inspection; anycast public IP rather than per-region DNS. Which front-end best fits all four?
choices: Azure Traffic Manager with priority routing
Azure Load Balancer Standard with cross-region frontends
Azure CDN Premium configured in front of both regions
Azure Front Door with a WAF policy
questions.explanation: Azure Front Door is a global Layer-7 edge service: anycast public IP, latency-based routing to the closest healthy origin, automatic failover on origin health probes, TLS termination at the edge, and Azure WAF integrated for OWASP rule enforcement. Traffic Manager is DNS-based — it returns the address of an endpoint to the resolver and never sees the HTTP request, so no edge TLS or WAF. Load Balancer Standard is regional Layer-4 and has no global anycast frontend. Azure CDN focuses on caching and does not provide the same edge-WAF feature Front Door does.

questions.q: VMs in an app subnet need OUTBOUND internet connectivity (e.g., to update servers, call SaaS APIs) without each VM having its own public IP. NO inbound from internet is required. The solution must be (a) managed-PaaS, (b) high-throughput, (c) without per-VM NIC public IPs. Which Azure service?
choices: Azure Load Balancer Standard with outbound rules on the subnet
Azure Firewall in a hub VNet attached to a dedicated subnet
An Azure NAT Gateway attached to the subnet
A public IP assigned to every VM NIC in the subnet
questions.explanation: NAT Gateway is the managed, outbound-only NAT for a subnet: VMs share its public IPs for egress, no inbound exposure is created, and the SNAT port budget is far higher than what Load Balancer outbound rules give before exhaustion at scale. Load Balancer outbound rules work but were sized for combined inbound/outbound and exhaust SNAT ports under high concurrency. Azure Firewall provides egress with packet inspection, which is heavy-weight when the scenario has no inspection requirement. Assigning a public IP per NIC is exactly what the scenario forbids.

correct.useCase: Stateful allow/deny rules that filter inbound and outbound traffic for Azure subnets and network interfaces.

distractors.useCase: Routes traffic between on-premises and Azure over ExpressRoute.
Automatically scales VM instances based on load.
Assigns a role to a user for a specific resource.

nodes.title: Compute services: Key Ideas
nodes.content: 'Compute' is everything that runs your code: VMs, containers, serverless functions, batch jobs. The exam wants you to pick the right shape — long-running stateful workload → VM, packaged app → container, event-driven short job → serverless.

flashcards.front: VM vs container vs serverless — pick a service for each.
flashcards.back: VM (EC2 / Compute Engine / Azure VM) when you need full OS control. Container (ECS, GKE, AKS, Cloud Run) when you've packaged an app and want orchestration. Serverless (Lambda, Functions, Cloud Functions) for short event-driven tasks, no infrastructure to manage.

flashcards.front: What is autoscaling?
flashcards.back: A service that adds/removes compute instances based on a signal (CPU, request rate, queue depth, custom metric). Scale-out is cheap; scale-in saves money. Target tracking is the simplest mode: 'keep average CPU at 60%'.

flashcards.front: Spot / preemptible / low-priority — what's the catch?
flashcards.back: Up to 90% off list price, but the cloud can yank the instance with 30 s – 2 min warning. Use for fault-tolerant batch jobs, CI runners, big-data clusters. Don't use for stateful databases or anything that needs to stay up.

flashcards.front: Reserved / committed-use vs on-demand pricing.
flashcards.back: On-demand: pay by the hour or second, no commitment. Reserved / committed: 1-3 year commitment, 30-60% discount, no flexibility. Pick reserved for steady baseline load, on-demand for spiky workloads.

questions.q: Two Windows VMs host a web tier in a single region and must meet Microsoft's 99.95% VM SLA. The agreement requires protection against both planned host maintenance and unplanned hardware failures within the region. What is the MINIMUM configuration that meets 99.95%?
choices: Both VMs on Premium SSD managed disks with read-cache enabled
Both VMs in two regions fronted by Azure Traffic Manager DNS
Both VMs in a single Availability Zone with Premium SSD disks
Both VMs in an Availability Set across fault and update domains
questions.explanation: Two or more VMs in an Availability Set are spread across distinct fault and update domains, hitting Microsoft's 99.95% in-region VM SLA — that is the minimum SLA configuration. Premium SSD covers a separate disk SLA and does not affect the compute SLA. Multi-region Traffic Manager is a disaster-recovery pattern that exceeds the in-region requirement at far higher cost. A single Availability Zone exposes the workload to a zone-wide failure and does not meet 99.95% on its own — you need at least two zones (which lands at the 99.99% zonal SLA, overkill for the minimum).

questions.q: An autoscale rule must launch 50 new D4s_v3 VMs (4 vCPUs each) in East US within minutes. The subscription's regional compute-quota for the new D-series VMs in East US currently allows only 100 vCPUs. The deployment fails on the 26th new VM. What's the right fix?
choices: Submit a quota-increase request for the D-series vCPU family in East US
Move the new VMs into a different resource group in the same subscription
Switch the new fleet to Azure Spot VMs to avoid the standard quota
Recreate the scale set in a different Azure region with the same workload
questions.explanation: Azure enforces vCPU quotas per VM family per region per subscription. Going from 100 to 200 vCPUs of D-series in East US requires a quota-increase request through Subscriptions → Usage + quotas. Resource groups are logical containers with no quota of their own — moving the VMs keeps the same subscription-level limit. Spot VMs draw from the same regional vCPU family quota, so they hit the same ceiling. Choosing a different region introduces its own (possibly equally low) regional quota and changes the workload's latency and data-residency posture rather than fixing the root cause.

questions.q: A team needs to run a SHORT-LIVED containerised data-processing job that completes in <10 minutes. Requirements: no cluster/infra to manage, per-second billing for the runtime, just submit the image and run. Which Azure service fits all three?
choices: Azure Kubernetes Service running the job in an existing node pool
Azure Container Instances with per-second billing
App Service Web App for Containers running the image
Azure Service Fabric scheduled task on the cluster
questions.explanation: Azure Container Instances runs a container without a cluster, bills per-second for the runtime, and starts in seconds — a precise fit for a sub-10-minute job. AKS requires a node pool whose VMs keep billing whether or not the job runs, and adds cluster operations. App Service for Containers is designed for long-running web workloads with monthly compute plans, not per-second runtime billing. Service Fabric is a cluster runtime — always-on node billing and significant operational footprint.

questions.q: A VM Scale Set autoscale-in event is triggered. One VMSS instance is halfway through a 3-hour batch job and must NOT be terminated. Other instances must remain eligible for scale-in. Which feature protects only that single instance?
choices: Apply ProtectFromScaleIn Instance Protection to the running instance
Switch the entire VMSS to manual scaling mode for the job's duration
Enable VMSS Scheduled Events with a 15-minute notification delay
Pin a static private IP to that instance's network interface
questions.explanation: Instance Protection has two flags. ProtectFromScaleIn excludes a single instance from autoscale-in decisions while letting the rest of the scale set scale normally — the precise scope the scenario needs. Switching the whole VMSS to manual scaling freezes scaling for every instance, which is over-broad. Scheduled Events only notifies the VM that a maintenance or eviction event is imminent so the workload can drain; it does not prevent the autoscale-in selection. A static IP affects networking, not scale-in eligibility.

questions.q: An ARM template deploys a Windows VM from a Marketplace image. After deployment the VM must automatically — with no user action — (a) join the corporate AD domain and (b) install an MSI package. The automation must fire on first boot, declaratively, from the template itself. Which option achieves this?
choices: RDP in after deployment and run the domain-join and install scripts manually
Add the Domain Join and Custom Script Extension VM extensions to the ARM template
Connect through Azure Bastion and run the join and install scripts interactively
Bake a Windows scheduled task into the source image that runs on first boot
questions.explanation: VM extensions declared in an ARM or Bicep template run automatically on first boot. The Domain Join Extension joins the AD domain, and Custom Script Extension downloads and installs the MSI — both are declarative, idempotent, and template-driven. Manual RDP or Bastion sessions are operator actions, not automation, and break repeatability. A scheduled task baked into the image is image-time customisation rather than template-driven automation, so the ARM template no longer controls the configuration.

questions.q: A VMSS autoscale rule (add 2 VMs when CPU > 75% for 10 minutes) is OSCILLATING — brief CPU spikes trigger scale-out, cooldown lets scale-in fire on quiet periods, and the pattern repeats. The daily traffic is highly predictable (busy 09:00-17:00 weekdays, idle otherwise). Which approach removes the oscillation while still scaling for the predictable load?
choices: Raise the CPU scale-out threshold from 75% to 95%
Switch to a schedule-based scaling profile by hour of day
Increase the autoscale cooldown period to 30 minutes
Remove the scale-in rule and keep only the scale-out rule
questions.explanation: When demand is predictable (09:00–17:00 weekdays busy, otherwise idle), schedule-based scaling profiles — for example, capacity 10 between 09:00 and 17:00, capacity 3 otherwise — set the right capacity directly and remove the metric-driven oscillation entirely. Raising the threshold keeps the reactive logic; transient spikes still trip it. Larger cooldowns slow the oscillation but do not address the wrong basis. Removing the scale-in rule prevents scale-down forever, which wastes capacity during the predictable idle window.

questions.q: A NON-CRITICAL batch workload CAN tolerate interruption (it checkpoints every 5 min and resumes elsewhere if evicted). The team wants the LARGEST possible cost discount on the compute. Which pricing model fits?
choices: Reserved Instance with a 1-year commitment
Azure Savings Plan for Compute with a 1-year commitment
Azure Spot VMs
Pay-as-you-go with auto-shutdown outside business hours
questions.explanation: Spot VMs trade availability for cost — Azure can evict them with about 30 seconds' notice and they price at up to ~90% off pay-as-you-go, exactly the deepest-discount tier for interruptible, checkpoint-friendly workloads. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans require a 1- or 3-year commitment to steady-state usage and target predictable workloads, not bursty interruptible ones. Pay-as-you-go with auto-shutdown does not discount the hourly compute rate; it only avoids billing during the off hours.

questions.q: Two VMs (an app server and a latency-sensitive database) must be deployed with the lowest possible inter-VM network latency in the same region. Same Availability Zone is not specific enough — within an AZ, VMs can sit in different physical buildings. Which Azure feature physically co-locates the VMs in the same data-centre row?
choices: Place both VMs in the same Azure Availability Set
Place both VMs in the same Azure Availability Zone
Place both VMs in the same Azure resource group
Place both VMs in the same Azure Proximity Placement Group
questions.explanation: A Proximity Placement Group is a scheduler hint that co-locates VMs in the same physical data-centre row or cluster, giving the lowest inter-VM network latency Azure offers. Availability Sets deliberately spread VMs across fault and update domains — the opposite goal. The same Availability Zone narrows region to a zone but the VMs can still land in different buildings within that zone. Resource groups are logical containers and have no placement effect on hardware.

nodes.title: Deploy a VM: build the dependency chain

data.scenario: Create the resources an Azure VM needs, in dependency order (each step needs the one before it).

nodes.explanation: An Azure VM depends on a chain: a resource group holds everything, a virtual network and subnet provide addressing, a network interface attaches the VM to the subnet, and finally the VM is created on that NIC.

nodes.title: Storage concepts: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud storage comes in three flavors with very different cost/perf trade-offs: object (think S3), block (think EBS / managed disks), and file (think EFS / Azure Files / Filestore). Pick wrong and you either overpay or hit performance ceilings.

flashcards.front: Object vs block vs file storage — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Object (S3, Blob, GCS) for unstructured data, backups, static sites, data lakes — flat namespace, HTTP API, infinite scale. Block (EBS, managed disks) for OS disks and databases — low latency, single attach. File (EFS, NFS) when multiple VMs need a shared POSIX filesystem.

flashcards.front: What is a storage class / tier?
flashcards.back: Same data, different SLA and price. Hot tier (frequent access, expensive read, cheap retrieval). Cold/archive tier (rare access, cheap to store, expensive to read, retrieval latency from minutes to hours). Lifecycle policies move data between tiers automatically.

flashcards.front: Why use server-side encryption?
flashcards.back: Data is encrypted at rest by the storage service using either provider-managed keys (default, no extra config) or your own keys via KMS. This protects against physical disk theft and meets compliance baselines without changing your app code.

flashcards.front: What's storage durability vs availability?
flashcards.back: Durability is the chance your data won't be lost (object stores claim ~11 9s — 99.999999999%). Availability is the chance you can reach it right now (typically 4 9s — 99.99%). Durability is multi-region replication; availability is how many concurrent failures the service tolerates.

questions.q: A latency-sensitive workload needs (a) consistent sub-millisecond disk latency, (b) up to 160 000 IOPS and 4 000 MB/s throughput, (c) the ability to ADJUST IOPS and throughput AT RUNTIME WITHOUT restarting the VM or detaching the disk. Which Azure managed disk SKU supports ALL three?
choices: Ultra Disk with provisioned IOPS and throughput
Premium SSD v2 at its largest size tier
Premium SSD v1 (P80) with read caching enabled
Standard SSD at its largest size tier
questions.explanation: Ultra Disk supports up to 160,000 IOPS and 4,000 MB/s per disk, offers sub-millisecond latency, and lets you adjust IOPS and throughput independently while the VM keeps running. Premium SSD v2 also exposes online-tunable IOPS and throughput, but its current per-disk ceilings sit below Ultra's top-end values the scenario calls out. Premium SSD v1 ties IOPS and throughput to fixed size tiers (P30, P50, P80…), so retuning requires resizing the disk. Standard SSD targets light workloads and cannot reach sub-millisecond latency or the IOPS the scenario requires.

questions.q: A company keeps 7-year compliance archives in Azure Blob Storage. Access frequency is near zero (occasional audit retrieval; hours of restore latency is acceptable). Minimum storage cost is the priority. Which blob access tier should they use?
choices: Hot
Archive
Cool
Cold
questions.explanation: Archive is the offline blob tier with the lowest per-GB storage cost; rehydration takes up to several hours, which fits the 'occasional audit, hours of latency acceptable' brief. Hot is for frequently accessed data and has the highest storage cost. Cool sits between Hot and Archive — cheaper storage with a 30-day minimum and quick retrieval — but still costs more than Archive on cold data. Cold is cheaper than Cool with a 90-day minimum but remains online and is still more expensive than Archive when access is near zero.

questions.q: VMs in a VNet must access an Azure Storage account so that (a) traffic travels via the Azure backbone with a PRIVATE IP, (b) the storage account is reachable on a private DNS name from within the VNet, and (c) public storage endpoints can be blocked entirely. Which feature satisfies all three?
choices: A Storage Service Endpoint with a VNet rule on the storage account
A storage firewall rule with 'Allow trusted Azure services'
A Private Endpoint for the storage account in the VNet
A VPN Gateway with forced tunneling enabled on the VNet
questions.explanation: A Private Endpoint deploys a NIC with a private IP into the VNet that maps to the storage account; DNS resolves the storage FQDN to that private IP, and the storage firewall can be set to deny all public traffic. A Service Endpoint keeps traffic on the backbone but leaves a public endpoint on the storage account and assigns no private IP into the VNet. The 'Allow trusted Azure services' exception lets specific Microsoft services bypass the firewall — it does nothing for VM-originated traffic. Forced tunneling sends VPN traffic over a custom egress and has no role in reaching PaaS storage privately.

questions.q: A high-performance computing (HPC) application requires shared file storage accessible by hundreds of Linux VMs simultaneously via NFS v4.1, with consistent sub-millisecond latency and throughput of over 1,000 MB/s. Which Azure storage service is designed for this workload?
choices: Azure Files Premium with the SMB protocol
Azure NetApp Files using NFS 4.1
Azure shared managed disks in shared mode
Azure Blob Storage exposed over NFS 3.0
questions.explanation: Azure NetApp Files is an enterprise NAS service built on NetApp hardware; the Ultra service level provides sub-millisecond latency and 128 MB/s per provisioned TiB, scaling linearly to satisfy 1,000+ MB/s when sized appropriately. It natively supports NFS 3 and NFS 4.1 — the exact protocol the workload uses. Azure Files Premium is primarily SMB; NFS 4.1 is supported but with lower throughput ceilings than NetApp Files. Shared managed disks expose block storage to a small cluster, not a POSIX filesystem for hundreds of NFS clients. Blob NFS 3.0 targets read-heavy object workloads and does not deliver the consistent sub-millisecond latency for HPC writes.

questions.q: A Windows dev team needs to share config files and binaries across multiple Azure VMs via SMB 3.x, with Active-Directory-DS authentication (not just a storage-account key), and a fully managed service (no file-server VM to operate). Which storage service fits all three?
choices: Azure Files (Standard or Premium) with AD DS authentication
Azure NetApp Files SMB 3.x volumes with AD DS authentication
Azure Blob Storage exposed over NFS 3.0
Azure shared managed disks attached to the VMs
questions.explanation: Azure Files is the managed SMB file share: it speaks SMB 3.x, supports identity-based access through on-prem AD DS (or Azure AD DS), and is fully managed — no file server VM to operate. Azure NetApp Files also supports SMB with AD DS but is enterprise NAS for high-performance workloads at premium pricing, more than the scenario calls for. Blob NFS 3.0 targets Linux and has no SMB or AD DS authentication. Shared managed disks expose block storage with no SMB or file-level authentication semantics.

questions.q: An external partner needs READ access to a SPECIFIC blob container for 48 hours, after which the access must expire automatically. The grant must be (a) scoped to that container only, (b) auto-expiring, (c) NOT require the partner have a Microsoft account, (d) NEVER expose your storage account key. Which mechanism?
choices: Share the storage account access key with the partner
Generate a Shared Access Signature scoped to the container with 48-hour expiry
Create an Azure AD Guest user and assign Storage Blob Data Reader on the container
Enable anonymous public read access scoped to the container
questions.explanation: A Shared Access Signature can be scoped to a single container, restricted to read, time-bound to 48 hours, and signed with either a storage-account key or — better — a user-delegation key. The partner needs no Microsoft account, and the storage-account key never leaves the tenant. Sharing the storage account key grants full control of the entire account and is a known security anti-pattern. A Guest user works but requires the partner to have a Microsoft identity and the grant does not auto-expire after 48 hours. Anonymous public read exposes the container to the entire internet, not only the partner.

questions.q: Blobs older than 90 days must move to Cool, blobs older than 365 days must move to Archive, and blobs older than 7 years must be deleted. The team wants a declarative policy, not custom code or runbooks. Which Azure Storage feature delivers this?
choices: An Azure Data Factory pipeline triggered by blob storage events
Azure Blob versioning combined with a storage retention policy
An Azure Storage lifecycle management policy
An Azure Automation runbook on a daily schedule calling the SDK
questions.explanation: Lifecycle management policies are the storage-native, declarative way to age blobs: JSON rules filter by prefix or blob type and act on 'days since last modified' to transition tiers (to Cool, Cold, Archive) or delete the blob. Policies run daily at no extra cost. Versioning controls how many revisions are kept, not where data lives. A Data Factory pipeline or an Automation runbook can re-implement the behaviour with custom code, but the storage service ships the declarative feature for this exact scenario.

nodes.title: Identity providers and federation: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Modern identity is centralized — one identity provider issues tokens that every application trusts. SAML and OIDC are the two interop standards. Federation means trusting another organization's identity provider for cross-org access.

flashcards.front: SAML vs OIDC — what's the practical difference?
flashcards.back: SAML: XML, browser-redirect-heavy, used for enterprise SSO into web apps. OIDC (on top of OAuth 2.0): JSON, mobile- and SPA-friendly, the modern default. New integrations should use OIDC; existing SAML works fine, no urgent reason to migrate.

flashcards.front: What's an IdP vs an SP (service provider)?
flashcards.back: Identity Provider: where users actually authenticate (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, Auth0). Service Provider: the app the user is trying to use (Slack, Salesforce, your custom app). The IdP issues a signed token; the SP trusts the IdP's signature and reads the user's identity from the token.

flashcards.front: MFA — why is push notification preferred over SMS?
flashcards.back: SMS is sniffable (SS7 attacks) and SIM-swappable. Push (Duo, Microsoft Authenticator, OS-level biometric) is bound to a specific device, requires user interaction, harder to phish. WebAuthn / FIDO2 hardware keys are the gold standard — phishing-resistant by design.

flashcards.front: Just-in-time (JIT) provisioning — what does it solve?
flashcards.back: Instead of pre-creating users in every app, JIT creates the user on first SSO login, hydrated from the IdP's attributes. Onboarding a new hire: add to the IdP group once, every app that supports JIT auto-creates them on first visit. Deprovisioning is the inverse — IdP removes them, apps refuse next login.

questions.q: An organisation runs on-prem Active Directory and wants employees to sign in to Microsoft 365 with their on-prem credentials, with PASSWORD VALIDATION HAPPENING AGAINST THE ON-PREM AD DOMAIN CONTROLLER (no password hashes synced to Azure AD). Which Azure AD Connect sign-in method fits this constraint?
choices: Password Hash Synchronization (PHS) as the sign-in method
Pass-through Authentication (PTA) with on-prem agents
Federation with an on-prem AD FS farm
Azure AD Connect cloud sync with PHS as the sign-in method
questions.explanation: Pass-through Authentication runs a lightweight agent on-premises that receives each Azure AD sign-in request, validates the password against the local domain controller, and returns the result — no password hash is ever stored in Azure AD. PHS synchronises a hash of the password hash to Azure AD and validates against that copy, which violates the 'no hashes synced' requirement. AD FS also keeps authentication on-prem but requires a dedicated federation farm, which the scenario rules out as heavyweight. Cloud sync uses the cloud provisioning agent, but the actual sign-in method behind it is still PHS, so it fails the same 'no hash sync' constraint.

questions.q: A Conditional Access policy requires MFA when users sign in from OUTSIDE the corporate network (corporate IP range added as a Trusted Named Location with MFA exclusion). A user signs in from the office (within the trusted IP range) and is NOT challenged for MFA. The admin confirms this is expected behaviour. Why?
choices: MFA is mandatory regardless of location; the bypass must be a configuration mistake
MFA was completed within the past 24 hours on another corporate device
The user's session was deemed fresh enough to skip the MFA challenge
The policy excludes the trusted Named Location from the MFA condition
questions.explanation: The Conditional Access policy condition uses a Trusted Named Location to exclude the corporate IP range, so sign-ins from that range never meet the MFA condition — the documented, expected behaviour. CA conditions evaluate signals at sign-in; if the location does not match, the control simply does not apply. There is no automatic 'fresh session' bypass that ignores MFA. Conditional Access can remember MFA for a sign-in frequency window, but that records a satisfied MFA claim rather than silently skipping the prompt and would not be tied to the corporate IP range.

questions.q: An organisation wants security administrators to hold Global Administrator only when actively needed, with: explicit activation request, just-in-time elevation, optional approval workflow, and full audit trail of every activation. Which Azure AD feature fits all four?
choices: Azure AD Conditional Access session controls
Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
Azure RBAC time-bound role assignments via JSON definitions
Azure AD custom role definitions scoped through administrative units
questions.explanation: Privileged Identity Management makes a role 'eligible' rather than 'active' — users request activation, optionally pass an approval workflow, satisfy MFA, and the role expires automatically; every activation is audited. Conditional Access session controls gate existing sessions but do not surface a role activation workflow. Time-bound RBAC assignments expire a role after a fixed window but do not require an explicit activation request or approval. Custom role definitions shape the permission set only; they do not provide just-in-time activation.

questions.q: Employees of a partner company (a different Azure AD tenant) need access to SharePoint and Azure resources in our tenant, signing in with their own corporate credentials. We will not create local accounts and we will not merge tenants. Which Azure AD feature meets the requirement?
choices: Azure AD B2C with a custom user-flow policy
Azure AD Connect cloud sync mirroring the partner directory
Local Azure AD accounts provisioned per partner user
Azure AD B2B Collaboration with Guest accounts
questions.explanation: B2B Collaboration invites users from another Azure AD tenant (or other supported identity providers) into our tenant as Guests; they authenticate in their home tenant and our tenant authorises them through standard RBAC. No local accounts are created and the tenants stay separate. B2C is the consumer-identity product for customer-facing apps with custom branded sign-in. Cloud sync mirrors on-premises Active Directory into Azure AD — it cannot mirror another Azure AD tenant. Provisioning local accounts is exactly what the scenario excludes.

questions.q: A user attempts self-service password reset and gets 'feature not enabled'. The admin needs the per-user / group / all-users setting that turns on SSPR for the tenant. Which feature is this?
choices: Azure AD Self-Service Password Reset (SSPR)
Azure AD MFA registration policy
Azure AD Password Protection global banned list
Azure AD Identity Protection sign-in risk policy
questions.explanation: Self-Service Password Reset is the named feature toggled in Azure AD → Password reset, scoped to None, Selected, or All users. Until SSPR is enabled, end users see the 'feature not enabled' message. The MFA registration policy enrols users in MFA methods but does not turn on SSPR. Password Protection blocks weak or banned passwords at change time but cannot enable the self-service flow. Identity Protection sign-in risk policies challenge or block risky sign-ins; they are unrelated to enabling the SSPR feature.

questions.q: A Conditional Access policy must BLOCK legacy authentication protocols (IMAP, POP3, SMTP AUTH, MAPI) because they bypass MFA. The policy must apply to all users and all cloud apps. Which condition + control combination achieves this?
choices: Condition: all cloud apps; Control: Require MFA
Condition: Client apps = Legacy authentication clients; Control: Block access
Condition: Sign-in risk = High; Control: Require MFA
Condition: Device platform = Unknown; Control: Block access
questions.explanation: The Client apps condition in Conditional Access can target the legacy authentication client category (basic-auth flows used by older IMAP, POP, SMTP AUTH and MAPI clients) — pairing it with Block access stops those sign-ins outright. Requiring MFA does not help because basic-auth protocols cannot present an MFA challenge — they simply fail without remediation. Sign-in risk targets compromised behaviour rather than the legacy protocol family. Filtering by unknown device platform is over-broad and also blocks modern authentication on unrecognised devices.

questions.q: An organisation registering Azure AD MFA methods wants the most phishing-resistant option Microsoft offers — one that cryptographically binds the authentication to the relying-party origin, so a phishing site cannot capture a usable credential. Which method does Microsoft classify as phishing-resistant?
choices: SMS one-time passcode
Microsoft Authenticator push with number matching
FIDO2 security keys or platform passkeys
Phone-call approval with PIN confirmation
questions.explanation: FIDO2 security keys (and platform passkeys / Windows Hello for Business) are public-key methods that cryptographically bind the credential to the relying-party origin — a phishing site at a different origin cannot capture or replay a usable credential. Microsoft Authenticator push with number matching is strong and resists basic push-bombing, but it is not in Microsoft's phishing-resistant tier because the user can still be deceived into approving a relay. SMS OTPs and phone-call OTPs are explicitly classed as not phishing-resistant — attacker-in-the-middle proxies can capture and replay either.

nodes.title: Observability and monitoring: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Observability is metrics + logs + traces — the three pillars. You need all three to debug a production incident: metrics tell you something is wrong, logs tell you what happened, traces tell you where in the call graph the problem lives.

flashcards.front: Metrics vs logs vs traces — what does each tell you?
flashcards.back: Metrics: numeric time-series, cheap to store, perfect for dashboards and alerts ('p99 latency = 800 ms'). Logs: discrete events with context, expensive at scale, perfect for forensics. Traces: causally-linked spans showing a request's full path through services.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between an alert and a notification?
flashcards.back: An alert is a condition that fires when a metric crosses a threshold (CPU > 80% for 5 min). The notification is the resulting message (email, Slack, PagerDuty page). One alert can fan out to many notifications. Tuning alerts is harder than wiring notifications.

flashcards.front: What is an SLI / SLO / SLA?
flashcards.back: SLI (indicator): the metric you actually measure ('% of requests under 200 ms'). SLO (objective): the internal target ('99.9% of requests under 200 ms over 28 days'). SLA (agreement): the contractual promise to customers, usually weaker than the SLO so you have buffer.

flashcards.front: Why structured logs?
flashcards.back: Plain-text logs are unparseable at scale. Structured logs (JSON, with timestamp + level + service + request_id + key fields) are indexable, queryable, and join-able across services. Most platforms auto-extract fields from JSON without configuration.

questions.q: An admin needs a SINGLE service that ingests Azure VM perf counters, Azure Activity Log entries, AKS container logs, and Application Insights traces, then lets them join across those tables with KQL queries. Which Azure component fits?
choices: An Azure Log Analytics workspace
An Azure Monitor Metrics Explorer view
An Azure Application Insights resource
An Azure Event Hubs namespace
questions.explanation: A Log Analytics workspace is the unified log store: Activity Log, VM diagnostic logs, AKS container logs, and Application Insights telemetry can all be routed into one workspace and joined across tables with KQL. Metrics Explorer charts numeric metrics — it has no log tables and no KQL log-join. Application Insights is application telemetry only and is narrower than the multi-source unified log store the scenario asks for. Event Hubs is a high-throughput ingestion pipeline and a streaming target, not a queryable log store.

questions.q: An admin must stream Azure VM resource logs + platform metrics to BOTH (a) a 3rd-party SIEM via Event Hub in real time AND (b) an Azure Storage account for long-term archive. The mechanism is configured per-resource, natively. Which feature?
choices: Azure Monitor Agent with data collection rules
An Azure Automation runbook on a recurring schedule
Azure Diagnostic Settings on the resource
A Logic App triggered by Azure Monitor alerts
questions.explanation: Diagnostic Settings on a resource are the native fan-out: each setting can stream platform logs and metrics into any combination of Log Analytics, Storage, Event Hub (the SIEM ingestion point), and partner solutions — configured per resource. Azure Monitor Agent collects guest-OS telemetry; it does not fan-out platform diagnostic events to multiple sinks. An Automation runbook would have to script and schedule the export, which is not the native real-time mechanism. A Logic App on an alert handles event-driven workflows, not a continuous diagnostic stream.

questions.q: A security audit asks who deleted a production VM yesterday at 14:47 UTC and from which IP. The investigation must rely on a tenant-wide, immutable, default-on plane-of-record log. Which Azure log is the authoritative source?
choices: The Azure Activity Log for the subscription
The VM's Boot Diagnostics console output
Network Watcher NSG flow log archives
Application Insights request and trace logs
questions.explanation: The Azure Activity Log is the immutable, default-on, tenant-wide record of management-plane operations: every create, modify, and delete is logged with caller (UPN or service principal), timestamp, source IP, and result — the canonical 'who deleted what, when' source. Boot Diagnostics captures console output from a single VM and is unrelated to control-plane events. NSG flow logs record allowed and denied L4 flows on a subnet or NIC, not Resource Manager operations. Application Insights records application-side telemetry from instrumented code; it has no visibility into Azure resource lifecycle.

questions.q: An Azure Monitor metric alert fires when a VM scale set's average CPU exceeds 85% for 5 minutes. The team needs the alert to also (a) email two on-call DLs, (b) post to a webhook, (c) run a Logic App. Where is the email + webhook + Logic App configured — separately from the alert condition?
choices: In the alert rule's condition settings page
In an Azure Monitor diagnostic setting on the resource
In the scale set's autoscale rule
In an Action Group associated with the alert rule
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor splits alert design into two pieces: the alert rule defines when to fire (metric, threshold, evaluation window) and an Action Group defines what happens when it fires (email, SMS, webhook, Logic App, Azure Function, Automation runbook, ITSM connector). Multiple alert rules can share one Action Group, which is exactly the reuse pattern the scenario implies. The condition settings page chooses signal and threshold, not delivery. Diagnostic settings route raw logs, not alerts. Autoscale rules add or remove instances; they do not deliver notifications.

questions.q: An admin wants a shared, persistent, drag-and-drop visual surface in the Azure portal that combines (a) Log Analytics KQL query tiles, (b) Azure Monitor metric charts, (c) resource health tiles for selected resources. The artefact should be portal-resident and pinnable, not a workbook with parameter-driven interactivity. Which artefact?
choices: A shared Azure portal dashboard (drag-and-drop, pinnable)
The Azure Monitor Alerts summary blade
An Azure Monitor Workbook
The Log Analytics workspace overview blade
questions.explanation: A shared Azure portal dashboard is the drag-and-drop, pinnable surface that combines tiles from many resources — KQL query tiles, metric charts, resource health tiles — and persists for the team. Workbooks are interactive, parameter-driven reports — a different artefact whose interactivity the scenario explicitly says it does not need. The Alerts summary blade lists alerts only and is not a customisable visual canvas. The Log Analytics overview blade is scoped to one workspace and is not a cross-resource pinnable surface.

nodes.title: Cloud governance: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Governance is the set of policies and guardrails that keep a cloud account safe and on-budget as it scales from one engineer to a hundred. Think tagging standards, budget alerts, organizational policies, and the multi-account strategy.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple accounts (an Organization) instead of one big account?
flashcards.back: Blast-radius isolation: a compromised prod account doesn't leak into dev. Billing clarity: per-team or per-environment cost reports. Quota independence: prod doesn't share API limits with sandbox. Service Control Policies (AWS) / management groups (Azure) enforce 'no one can disable CloudTrail' across the whole org.

flashcards.front: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP)?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions any IAM identity in a member account can have. Even if a user's IAM policy grants `s3:*`, an SCP denying `s3:DeleteBucket` overrides it. SCPs are guardrails, not grants — they only restrict.

flashcards.front: Tagging strategy — name three high-leverage tags.
flashcards.back: (1) Owner / team — who pays and who to page. (2) Environment (prod/staging/dev) — drives access controls and lifecycle. (3) Cost-center / project — for chargeback. Tags are free and infinitely valuable for cost allocation and automation; enforce them with policies.

flashcards.front: What is a landing zone?
flashcards.back: A pre-baked multi-account setup with security baselines: org with master + audit + log-archive + workload accounts, CloudTrail / Config enabled everywhere, SSO wired up, network templates ready. AWS Control Tower / Azure Landing Zones / GCP setup automate this so you start on a safe foundation, not bare cloud.

questions.q: A compliance team needs to apply 30 related Azure Policy definitions (CIS benchmark) to a management group AS A SINGLE GROUPED UNIT — one assignment, one set of parameters, one compliance report. Re-assigning the 30 individually means 30 assignments to maintain. Which feature provides 'package of definitions' semantics?
choices: Assign each of the 30 definitions individually to the management group
An Azure Policy initiative (policy set definition)
A custom Azure Policy definition with all 30 rules in one JSON file
An Azure Blueprint that pins each definition as an artifact
questions.explanation: An Azure Policy initiative — also called a policy set — bundles many definitions into a single assignable unit and reports compliance as one combined score; built-in CIS, NIST 800-53, PCI-DSS, and ISO 27001 initiatives ship the same way. Assigning each definition individually creates 30 separate assignments to manage and matches the anti-pattern the scenario rejects. A custom definition cannot embed 30 independent rule logics in one JSON schema. Azure Blueprints bundles policy assignments alongside RBAC and templates and is being deprecated in favour of Deployment Stacks — the initiative is the right primitive for the 'package of definitions' requirement.

questions.q: An admin accidentally deleted a critical RG. The team wants to prevent any future deletion of that RG without revoking any user's RBAC role and without writing custom policy. Which Azure feature is purpose-built for this?
choices: A ReadOnly lock applied at the resource group scope
A ReadOnly lock applied to each resource individually
A deny assignment at the subscription level
A CanNotDelete lock at the resource group scope
questions.explanation: A CanNotDelete lock at the resource group blocks every delete operation across the RG and its resources — even Owners cannot delete until the lock is removed — while still allowing reads and updates. Resource Manager locks sit above RBAC, so no role changes are needed. A ReadOnly lock on the RG would also block writes, which is heavier than required. ReadOnly locks per resource are even more fragile and still block legitimate updates. Deny assignments are an internal mechanism used by Blueprints and Managed Apps; customers cannot author them directly the way they configure locks.

questions.q: Azure Policy enforces that every resource in a subscription MUST have a `CostCenter` tag. A new storage account is created with no tag — the deployment FAILS with a policy-violation error rather than silently logging. Which Policy effect produces this immediate-fail behaviour?
choices: Audit
Deny
Modify
DeployIfNotExists
questions.explanation: The Deny effect rejects a resource at submission time when the policy condition fails — exactly the immediate-fail behaviour the scenario describes. Audit logs the non-compliance but lets the deployment succeed. Modify changes the resource on the way through, typically adding a missing tag with a default value, so the deployment succeeds rather than fails. DeployIfNotExists triggers a separate post-deployment task to deploy a related resource — it does not block the initial submission.

questions.q: An enterprise has dozens of subscriptions under nested management groups. The CISO requires a policy that EVERY existing subscription AND every future subscription must inherit, with a SINGLE assignment to maintain. Which scope satisfies the requirement?
choices: Assign the policy to each subscription individually
Assign the policy at each resource group scope
Assign the policy at the Tenant Root Management Group
Configure the rule in Microsoft Defender for Cloud's posture engine
questions.explanation: Azure Policy assignments inherit downward through the management-group hierarchy, so an assignment at the Tenant Root MG applies to every current subscription and, automatically, every future subscription created under that tenant — one assignment, no future maintenance. Per-subscription assignments need to be re-applied to each new subscription, which the scenario explicitly rejects. Resource group scope is below subscription level and does not inherit upward to new subscriptions. Defender for Cloud has its own recommendations engine; configuring a rule there does not translate into an Azure Policy assignment across subscriptions.

questions.q: An organisation wants to enforce a STANDARD packaged Azure environment for every new project: a defined set of RBAC role assignments + resource groups + Policy assignments + ARM templates, deployed as a single VERSIONED package. New projects pick a version of the package. Which AZURE-NATIVE feature was purpose-built for this 'enterprise environment template' role?
choices: ARM templates alone deployed per project
An Azure Policy initiative grouping the policies only
A Terraform module shared across projects via remote state
Azure Blueprints (or its successor, Deployment Stacks)
questions.explanation: Azure Blueprints — being superseded by Deployment Stacks — is the Azure-native, versioned package of RBAC role assignments, resource groups, Azure Policy assignments, and ARM templates assigned as a single environment. New projects pick a published version. ARM templates alone cover resource deployment but not RBAC and policy as a packaged unit. A Policy initiative packages policies only — no RBAC, RGs, or ARM templates in the bundle. Terraform modules can re-implement the same pattern but are third-party tooling, not the Azure-native answer the scenario asks for.

nodes.title: Network operations (CompTIA Network+): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Network+ tests operational fundamentals: how SNMP works for device monitoring, why baseline documentation matters, the change-management process that prevents accidental outages, and syslog severity levels that tell you how serious a message is. These appear in scenario questions where you're asked which tool to use or which process was skipped.

flashcards.front: SNMP — OID, MIB, community string, v2c vs v3.
flashcards.back: OID (Object Identifier): a dotted-number path in the MIB tree that uniquely identifies one piece of device data (e.g., `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10` = ifInOctets). MIB (Management Information Base): the schema/dictionary that maps OIDs to human-readable names. Community string: a plain-text password used for SNMP v1/v2c authentication — typically 'public' (read) and 'private' (write); a well-known security weakness. SNMPv3 replaces community strings with proper user-based auth (MD5/SHA) and encryption (AES/DES).

flashcards.front: Why is network baseline documentation critical?
flashcards.back: A baseline records normal traffic volumes, CPU/memory levels, error rates, and routing tables — captured during a known-good period. When something goes wrong, you compare current readings to the baseline to spot the anomaly (utilization spiked 300%, a new route appeared, error rate tripled). Without a baseline, 'high CPU' is meaningless because you don't know what 'normal' was. Network+ expects you to identify baselining as a best practice before troubleshooting.

flashcards.front: Change management process — what are the key steps?
flashcards.back: Request change → assess risk and impact → obtain approval (CAB or manager) → schedule a maintenance window → implement → test and verify → document outcome → close. The exam distinguishes emergency changes (faster approval path for critical incidents) from standard changes (pre-approved, low-risk, routine). Skipping change management is the most common cause of self-inflicted outages.

flashcards.front: Syslog severity levels 0–7 — name them.
flashcards.back: 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice, 6 Informational, 7 Debug. Lower number = more severe. Most organizations alert on 0–3 and log 0–6. Debug (7) produces enormous volume and is usually enabled only during active troubleshooting. The mnemonic: Every Awful Crisis Erodes Wisdom, No Debate.

questions.q: Windows VMs in Azure must AUTOMATICALLY have a specific set of Windows features installed + services running. When a VM drifts from this in-OS configuration (someone disables a service, uninstalls a feature), the platform must AUTOMATICALLY restore it. Which Azure service runs the drift-detection-and-correction agent INSIDE the guest OS?
choices: Azure Automation Desired State Configuration / Guest Configuration
Azure Policy with the DeployIfNotExists effect
Azure Update Manager maintenance configurations
Custom Script Extension assigned per VM at deploy time
questions.explanation: Desired State Configuration (now part of Guest Configuration) runs an agent inside the guest OS that continuously evaluates the declared configuration and remediates drift — services restarted, features re-added, registry keys reset. DeployIfNotExists creates missing Azure-RM resources; it operates at the management plane and does not run inside the VM. Update Manager patches the OS on a schedule but does not enforce service or feature state. Custom Script Extension runs once at deploy time and has no continuous remediation loop.

questions.q: An ops team needs to schedule monthly OS-security patching on a fleet of Azure VMs (Windows + Linux) during a maintenance window every last Sunday 02:00-06:00. The chosen service must support recurring schedules, multi-VM scope (subscription / management group / tag selectors), and per-classification (Critical / Security) patch picking. Which service fits?
choices: Azure Automation Update Management (classic)
Hotpatch-enabled Windows Server Azure Edition auto-patching
Azure Update Manager maintenance configurations
An Azure Policy assignment with the audit effect on patch state
questions.explanation: Azure Update Manager is the current patching service: maintenance configurations support recurring schedules (e.g., last Sunday 02:00–06:00), broad scopes (subscription, management group, tag selector), and classification-based picks like Critical and Security. Update Management (classic) is the predecessor and is being retired in favour of Update Manager. Hotpatch on Windows Server Azure Edition installs patches without reboots but uses Microsoft-defined rings — admins do not pick the monthly window. An Azure Policy audit effect only flags non-compliant patch state; it does not orchestrate patching.

questions.q: Dev VMs marked with the metadata `Environment: Dev` must start every weekday at 07:00 and stop at 19:00 to save cost. The schedule is recurring, the VM selection is by that label, and the solution must avoid bespoke infrastructure. Which Azure feature fits best?
choices: Azure Logic Apps with a recurrence trigger
Azure Policy with a DeployIfNotExists effect
An Azure DevOps pipeline triggered by a cron schedule
Azure Automation runbook with a schedule and tag query
questions.explanation: An Azure Automation runbook (PowerShell or Python) hosted in an Automation Account can run on a schedule, query Azure for VMs by tag, and call Start-AzVM / Stop-AzVM — the no-bespoke-infrastructure pattern Microsoft documents for this scenario. Logic Apps can express the same workflow but cost more per execution and add an extra service to the cost surface. Azure Policy enforces configuration compliance; it has no scheduling primitive that calls VM operations. A DevOps pipeline works but couples a routine cost-saving operation to the build system and licensing, which is operationally over-broad.

questions.q: A production Azure VM is unresponsive — RDP and SSH fail, the VM agent is unreachable, even Azure Bastion can't connect. The admin needs to reach the VM's console (the equivalent of plugging a serial cable into a physical machine) to see boot output and run recovery commands. Which Azure feature provides this?
choices: Azure Bastion Standard tier with a shareable link
A Run Command extension issued through the portal
Re-image the VM from a recent custom snapshot
The Azure Serial Console with Boot Diagnostics enabled
questions.explanation: Serial Console attaches to the VM's COM1 / serial port via the hypervisor and the portal, so it works even when the OS network stack is hung — provided Boot Diagnostics is enabled to expose the console stream. Bastion proxies RDP and SSH and depends on the VM's network stack being responsive. Run Command sends scripts through the VM agent, which is also unreachable when the agent itself is down. Re-imaging from snapshot is destructive — it replaces the VM rather than letting you see boot output or run recovery commands.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: An app behind a STANDARD-tier Application Gateway is being SQL-injected. The team wants to block injection patterns at the load-balancer tier (no app-code change). The Standard SKU does NOT include WAF. Which upgrade enables a managed OWASP rule set in front of the app?
choices: Add NSG rules to the Application Gateway subnet blocking attacker source IPs
Switch the WAF policy mode from Detection to Prevention on the existing Standard_v2 SKU
Enable Azure DDoS Network Protection on the Application Gateway's VNet
Upgrade the Application Gateway SKU from Standard_v2 to WAF_v2
questions.explanation: The Standard_v2 Application Gateway does not include the Web Application Firewall — you upgrade to the WAF_v2 SKU to enable managed OWASP rule sets that match and block SQL injection payloads. Switching policy modes is moot because the Standard_v2 SKU has no WAF policy to switch. Azure DDoS Network Protection guards against volumetric L3/L4 floods, not application-layer injection. NSG rules operate on IP/port, so they can block known attacker IPs but cannot inspect HTTP request bodies for SQLi patterns.

questions.q: Regulation requires Azure VM disks to be encrypted at TWO LAYERS: (a) at the storage platform layer, and (b) inside the guest OS itself. Which combination meets both layers?
choices: Server-Side Encryption with platform-managed keys only
A customer-managed storage account using manual key-based encryption
Azure Disk Encryption using BitLocker or dm-crypt on its own
SSE with platform-managed keys plus Azure Disk Encryption inside the guest
questions.explanation: Server-Side Encryption protects the disk at the Azure storage platform, and Azure Disk Encryption (BitLocker on Windows, dm-crypt on Linux) protects the OS-resident filesystem inside the guest — running both gives defence-in-depth across the two distinct layers the regulation requires. SSE alone only covers the storage platform layer. ADE alone only covers the guest layer. A manual key-based storage account does not encrypt inside the guest OS and is not the documented two-layer pattern.

questions.q: A CISO wants a SINGLE dashboard that surfaces (a) unpatched OS vulns per VM, (b) public-exposed storage accounts, (c) drift from CIS benchmarks, and (d) a numeric posture score that improves as recommendations are remediated. The score is the executive KPI. Which Azure feature is this?
choices: An Azure Monitor custom workbook
The Azure Policy compliance dashboard
Microsoft Defender for Cloud Secure Score
A Microsoft Sentinel workbook
questions.explanation: Microsoft Defender for Cloud provides Cloud Security Posture Management — a unified dashboard with recommendations across VMs (unpatched vulnerabilities), storage (public exposure), and benchmark drift (CIS, ISO, NIST), together with a numeric Secure Score that rises as recommendations are remediated. An Azure Monitor workbook is a build-it-yourself report; it does not ship with the recommendations engine or the named score. The Azure Policy compliance dashboard shows pass/fail counts per policy assignment but has no Secure Score. A Sentinel workbook is for SIEM analytics over event logs, not posture recommendations.

questions.q: An admin needs a single backup target supporting (a) Azure VM backup, (b) SQL Server in Azure VM backup, (c) on-prem Windows file servers via the MARS agent. Which Azure resource is the target for all three?
choices: A Backup vault (the newer SKU)
An Azure Storage account configured as the backup destination
A Recovery Services vault
A Site Recovery vault configured for VM replication
questions.explanation: A Recovery Services vault is the long-standing target for Azure VM backup, SQL-in-VM backup, MARS-agent backup of on-prem file servers, and ASR replication — one resource type covers all three workloads in the question. The newer Backup vault targets blob, disk, files, and PostgreSQL backups; it does not cover VM or MARS today. A raw storage account is not a valid backup destination — the Backup service writes through a vault that owns the underlying storage. 'Site Recovery vault' is the same resource type as Recovery Services vault but configured for replication; the question asks for the backup target.

questions.q: A regional ransomware incident has corrupted the in-region recovery points of a Recovery Services vault (the attacker had vault-contributor and triggered point deletion before locking the data). The vault is configured with cross-region geo-redundancy. Which recovery option uses the OUT-OF-REGION copy that the attacker could not reach?
choices: Instant Restore from a snapshot copy in the same region
File-level recovery mounting a 3-day-old disk from the same region
ASR failover into the paired region using the cross-region replica
Cross-Region Restore from the paired-region copy
questions.explanation: Cross-Region Restore reads the paired-region copy that Recovery Services vaults maintain when geo-redundant storage is enabled, so the restore source is outside the compromised region. Instant Restore reads in-region snapshots — the same surface the attacker corrupted. File-level recovery against an in-region recovery point relies on the same compromised data. Azure Site Recovery replicates running VMs for DR failover; it is a separate product and is not the recovery surface for backup recovery points.

questions.q: A VM backup policy must support: daily snapshots retained 30 days, weekly (Sunday) retained 12 weeks, monthly (1st Sunday) retained 18 months, yearly (1st Sunday of January) retained 7 years, AND multiple-backups-per-day. Which Azure VM backup policy SUBTYPE supports all of these in one policy?
choices: Enhanced backup policy with the Vault-Standard tier
Standard backup policy with the Enhanced tier subtype
Standard backup policy with daily-only recovery points
A custom backup policy authored through Azure Backup Center
questions.explanation: The Enhanced policy is the modern Azure VM backup policy type — it adds multiple backups per day on top of the GFS daily/weekly/monthly/yearly retention rules that long-term Standard policies already supported, all in one policy. The 'Standard policy with Enhanced subtype' description does not match any documented policy type. 'Standard policy with daily-only points' explicitly drops the weekly/monthly/yearly retention tiers the scenario requires. Backup Center is a portal-level management view, not a separate policy type — the underlying policy is still Standard or Enhanced, and only Enhanced supports the sub-daily cadence.

questions.q: A CI/CD pipeline builds container images and needs a private registry in Azure for distribution. Requirements: (a) Docker / OCI image format, (b) integrated AAD auth + managed identities, (c) geo-replicated across regions, (d) AKS / Container Apps pull-side support. Which Azure service?
choices: Azure Blob Storage with Docker layer caching
Azure Container Registry
Docker Hub private repository linked to AAD
The Azure Container Apps built-in image registry
questions.explanation: Azure Container Registry is the Azure-native, OCI-compliant private image registry: Entra ID integration with managed identities, geo-replication across regions on the Premium SKU, content trust, vulnerability scanning, and first-class AKS and Container Apps pull integration. Blob Storage is generic object storage — it does not implement the OCI registry protocol. Docker Hub is third-party SaaS and is not natively Entra ID-integrated with managed identities. Container Apps consumes images from ACR; it does not expose its own AAD-integrated registry.

questions.q: A DevOps team wants ACR to AUTOMATICALLY rebuild a container image when code is pushed to the GitHub repo source. The build should run inside ACR (no external CI runner) and push the resulting image into the same registry. Which feature?
choices: An Azure DevOps pipeline configured to push to ACR
AKS Flux GitOps continuous deployment
ACR Tasks with a Git source-code trigger
ACR geo-replication webhook trigger
questions.explanation: ACR Tasks lets you register a Git source — GitHub, Azure Repos, Bitbucket — and a Dockerfile path; on each push, ACR webhooks itself, builds the image on managed compute inside the registry, and pushes the result. An Azure DevOps pipeline compiles outside ACR on its own pipeline runner before pushing, which violates the 'no external CI runner' constraint. Flux deploys manifests pointing at already-built images; it does not build images. ACR geo-replication webhooks fire on push to keep replicas in sync — they do not build new images.
